summary: Defines a NAMESPACE command for IMAP4 that lets a client discover the prefixes servers use for personal mailboxes, other users' mailboxes, and shared mailboxes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2342 adds one command to IMAP4 so that a mail program can ask the server how it names its mailboxes. The server answers with the prefixes it uses for the user's own mailboxes, for other people's mailboxes and for shared mailboxes, which removes the need for users to type those prefixes in by hand.

subtitle: A command that lets a mail client ask a server which prefixes it uses for personal, shared and other users' mailboxes.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 does not define a default server namespace, so two different models grew up: some servers show only the user's own mailboxes, others show every mailbox the user can reach. A client cannot tell which, so users have to type the prefixes in by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a NAMESPACE command that returns the prefix and hierarchy delimiter for the personal, other users' and shared namespaces, and states how a client and a server should behave when there is more than one namespace of a kind.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2342 is a Proposed Standard from May 1998 and has been updated by RFC 4466.

today: RFC 2342 is a Proposed Standard from May 1998 and has been updated by RFC 4466. The NAMESPACE command it defines is the standard way for an IMAP client to learn the mailbox prefixes a server uses.

sections.title: The Problem with Default Namespaces
sections.content:
IMAP4, as defined in RFC 2060, does not define a default server namespace. Two models grew up as a result, and they behave differently.

In the Personal Mailbox model, the default namespace shown to the user contains only that user's own mailboxes, and reaching a shared mailbox needs an escape mechanism to cross into another namespace. In the Complete Hierarchy model, the default namespace contains the user's own mailboxes together with every other mailbox they have access to.

Both models create difficulties for certain client operations. The RFC's answer is a NAMESPACE command that lets a client discover the prefixes a server uses for personal mailboxes, for other users' mailboxes and for shared mailboxes. The goal is to remove much of the manual configuration that users now need when they mix and match IMAP4 clients and servers.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP4 says nothing about which mailboxes a server shows by default, so servers ended up with two different habits. A client that does not know which habit a server has cannot build the right mailbox names, and the user has to supply the missing prefixes by hand.

sections.title: The Three Namespace Kinds
sections.content:
The RFC defines three kinds of namespace. A Personal Namespace is the part of the namespace that belongs to the authenticated user on a given connection, and typically only that user can reach the mailboxes in it. If a user has an INBOX, it must appear within the user's personal namespace. In the typical case there should be only one Personal Namespace on a server.

An Other Users' Namespace holds mailboxes taken from the personal namespaces of other users. To reach them, the authenticated user must have been explicitly granted access rights, for example when a manager gives a secretary access to the manager's mailbox. In the typical case there should be only one Other Users' Namespace on a server. A Shared Namespace holds mailboxes meant to be shared among users, which do not exist within any user's personal namespace.

The namespaces a server uses may differ from one user to the next. In the examples, lines prefixed C: are sent by the client and lines prefixed S: by the server, and a line that is wrapped without a new label is wrapped only for the sake of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: A server's mailboxes fall into three groups: the ones belonging to the user, the ones belonging to other users that the user has been given access to, and the ones meant to be shared. The groups are reached through prefixes, and the prefixes can differ from user to user.

sections.title: What Clients Can Learn
sections.content:
Clients often want to create mailboxes of their own, such as one to keep a record of sent messages or one to hold a message being composed. To work with the range of IMAP4 servers in use, the user otherwise has to enter the prefix of the Personal Namespace by hand. With the NAMESPACE command, a client discovers that prefix on its own, with no manual configuration.

Users are also often made to type the prefixes of other namespaces in order to see the mailboxes in them, for example a prefix of #shared to reach the shared mailboxes. The command lets a client discover the namespaces a server has available, and then present them to the user in whatever way it likes: it could show only the personal mailboxes at first, or it could show the complete list of available mailboxes and start the user at the root of their Personal Namespace.

A server may choose to expose only a subset of the namespaces it supports. So that the user can still reach the ones left out, a client should let the user type a namespace prefix in by hand.
sections.plainLanguage: The command saves the user from typing prefixes by hand, both for the mailboxes a client creates itself and for the shared or other users' areas. A client can then show the user whatever list it likes. A server may hide some namespaces, so the client should still allow manual entry.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
A server that supports this extension must list the keyword NAMESPACE in its CAPABILITY response, so that a client can discover the support before it tries the command.

The command is valid in the Authenticated and Selected states, which are the two states in which the client has an identity on the server and can therefore be told about personal mailboxes.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that implements the command must advertise it in its capabilities list. The client may send the command only after it has logged in, and it may send it again while a mailbox is selected.

sections.title: The NAMESPACE Command and Its Response
sections.content:
The command takes no arguments. It returns an untagged NAMESPACE response holding the prefix and hierarchy delimiter of the server's Personal Namespaces, Other Users' Namespaces and Shared Namespaces that the server wishes to expose, in that order. A namespace class that is not available is reported as NIL, and response extensions may be included, with any extension that is not on the IETF standards track prefixed with X-. The result codes are OK for a completed command, NO for an error that stops the command completing, and BAD for an invalid argument.

The prefix string lets a client create personal mailboxes automatically, or list every mailbox in a namespace. A server that has a single personal namespace with no leading prefix and uses / as its hierarchy delimiter answers like this:

C: A001 NAMESPACE
S: * NAMESPACE (("" "/")) NIL NIL
S: A001 OK NAMESPACE command completed

A server with a personal namespace, an Other Users' Namespace and several shared namespaces answers with one entry per namespace, and the hierarchy delimiter may differ between them:

C: A001 NAMESPACE
S: * NAMESPACE (("" "/")) (("~" "/")) (("#shared/" "/") ("#public/" "/")("#ftp/" "/")("#news." "."))
S: A001 OK NAMESPACE command completed

There are more details about how the prefixes are used. Although a server will usually support only one Personal Namespace and one Other Users' Namespace, circumstances exist where there may be several, and a client must be prepared for that. If a client is set up to create a particular mailbox and it is not clear which Personal Namespace to create it in, the client should let the user choose, and only one copy of that mailbox is then created. The level of hierarchy below the Other Users' Namespace prefix should be the user name, as used by the IMAP4 LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE command.

A client can find the personal namespaces of other users that are available to it by appending % to the Other Users' Namespace prefix in a LIST command. A server may return the list of users, or may return only the users who have explicitly granted access, or may refuse the listing and require a user name to be included in the prefix instead. A prefix does not have to contain a hierarchy delimiter, since in some cases it is not needed. Finally, the RFC notes that the convention has been to start namespaces with the hash character, but such namespaces are not friendly to IMAP URLs, where the hash must be written as %23, so implementers may prefer prefixes without it.
sections.plainLanguage: The command takes no arguments and answers with three groups of prefixes in a fixed order: personal, other users' and shared. A group with nothing in it comes back as NIL. A client uses the prefixes to create mailboxes and to list what is there.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The response is written in the augmented Backus-Naur Form. A namespace is either NIL or a list of entries, where each entry is a prefix and a hierarchy delimiter, followed by any number of response extensions. A response extension is a name followed by a list of strings. The full response is the untagged word NAMESPACE followed by three namespace values, the first for the Personal Namespaces, the second for the Other Users' Namespaces and the third for the Shared Namespaces.

The RFC adds one detail about character encoding: following IMAP4 convention, any international string in the NAMESPACE response must be in the modified UTF-7 format defined in RFC 2060.
sections.plainLanguage: The response shape is given in a formal notation so that implementations agree exactly. It also repeats the IMAP rule that non-ASCII names inside the response are written in modified UTF-7.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There is one security point, and it concerns the listing of other users' mailboxes. When a client sends a LIST command that uses the Other Users' Namespace prefix, a server should not list users who have not granted list access to their personal mailboxes to the authenticated user.

The reason is that such a list could disclose confidential information about who is on the server, and it could give an attacker a starting point for a list of user accounts to try.
sections.plainLanguage: A server should not reveal which other accounts exist unless they have agreed to share their mailboxes. The list would otherwise tell an attacker who works where and which accounts to try.

left.title: Personal Mailbox model
left.desc: The default namespace shows only the user's own mailboxes. Other areas need an escape mechanism to reach.

right.title: Complete Hierarchy model
right.desc: The default namespace shows the user's own mailboxes together with every mailbox the user can reach.

viz.caption: THE THREE NAMESPACE CLASSES AND THE MAILBOXES UNDER THEM
EXAMPLE 5.4 FROM THE RFC: PERSONAL, OTHER USERS' AND SEVERAL SHARED NAMESPACES

data.title: The NAMESPACE exchange
data.code:
C: A001 NAMESPACE
S: * NAMESPACE (("" "/")) (("~" "/")) (("#shared/" "/")
   ("#public/" "/")("#ftp/" "/")("#news." "."))
S: A001 OK NAMESPACE command completed
